label: D-v2-kfree-openai-gpt-6-luna-rephrasing
question: Are NYC streets more dangerous during nighttime hours? Present a chart and a conclusion suitable for a news report.

options.denominator: Equal-length 12-hour day or night window over the dataset period; total counts, not exposure-adjusted rates
options.reason: Crash counts show the absolute reported crash burden in the two equal-length daily time windows.
options.answer: These data cannot establish whether streets are more dangerous per road-user exposure; NYC recorded 813,762 nighttime crashes versus 1,455,425 daytime crashes, about 44.1% fewer at night.
options.interpretation: This framing answers when more police-reported crashes occurred and shows greater daytime crash volume. Equal 12-hour windows make the clock-time comparison straightforward, but crash counts alone do not show risk per trip or per road user; the dataset lacks traffic exposure data.

options.metric: Share of crashes with at least one person injured or killed
options.denominator: All police-reported crashes in each period
options.reason: The crash-level injury-or-fatality share measures how often a reported crash resulted in human harm, regardless of crash volume.
options.answer: These data cannot establish whether streets are more dangerous per road-user exposure; 28.1% of nighttime crashes involved an injury or death versus 22.9% of daytime crashes, a 5.2-percentage-point difference.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether a crash was more likely to involve reported human harm at night and shows a higher share for nighttime crashes. It is a defensible crash-severity comparison because each crash is the denominator, but it does not account for how many people or vehicles were on the road, nor establish risk per trip.

options.denominator: All police-reported crashes in each period
options.reason: A crash-level fatality rate isolates the most severe recorded outcome and avoids confusing the higher daytime crash count with fatality severity.
options.answer: These data cannot establish whether streets are more dangerous per road-user exposure; fatal crashes occurred at 2.45 per 1,000 nighttime crashes versus 1.01 per 1,000 daytime crashes (about 2.4 times as high at night).
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether a reported crash was more likely to be fatal at night and shows a higher nighttime fatal-crash rate. It is a defensible measure of crash-level fatal severity, but does not estimate an individual road user's risk because traffic volume and road-user exposure are absent.

answer:
The data cannot establish whether streets are more dangerous per road-user exposure; NYC recorded 813,762 nighttime crashes versus 1,455,425 daytime crashes, about 44.1% fewer at night ([chart](out/option_1.png), [values](out/values_1.csv)).
The data cannot establish whether streets are more dangerous per road-user exposure; 28.1% of nighttime crashes involved an injury or death versus 22.9% of daytime crashes, a 5.2-percentage-point difference ([chart](out/option_2.png), [values](out/values_2.csv)).
The data cannot establish whether streets are more dangerous per road-user exposure; fatal crashes occurred at 2.45 per 1,000 nighttime crashes versus 1.01 per 1,000 daytime crashes, about 2.4 times as high at night ([chart](out/option_3.png), [values](out/values_3.csv)).
